_meta.source: Primary regulatory advisories (Panama Canal Authority), peer-reviewed attribution studies (World Weather Attribution, Marengo et al., Munoz et al.), USDA Grain Transportation Report, and Bolsa de Comercio de Rosario. Live transit counts are joined at render time from data/portwatch.json (IMF PortWatch, AIS-derived).
_meta.method: Each lane carries an ENSO PHASE and an ATTRIBUTION STRENGTH assessed separately. The phase is which side of ENSO has historically degraded that lane -- NOT an assumption that El Niño degrades all of them. Two of the four food-relevant inland waterways failed under LA NINA, not El Niño.
_meta.why_phase_matters: The single most common error in ENSO reporting is assuming every location moves the same direction. Applied to shipping it produces a specific false claim: that El Niño threatens the Mississippi and the Parana. It does not. The Mississippi's 2022 record low fell in a La Niña, and the Parana's 2019-21 record lows were attributed by World Weather Attribution chiefly to the triple-dip La Niña. Presenting these beside Panama under one 'at risk from El Niño' heading would be wrong.
_meta.attribution_scale: strong = a documented, source-attributed causal chain from ENSO phase to operational restriction. moderate = a real ENSO contribution that published attribution finds co-equal with or secondary to other forcing. weak = mechanism plausible and documented but no quantified disruption event. none = no credible ENSO link; listed so the page states the absence rather than leaving it implicit.
_meta.live_join: portwatch_key joins to data/portwatch.json data.<key> for transits_per_day, yoy and status. A lane with no portwatch_key is an inland waterway PortWatch does not cover -- its status is historical only and is labelled as such.

lanes.name: Panama Canal
lanes.food_role: About 29% of US soybean exports, 18% of maize and roughly 91% of sorghum normally transit here (MY2023, American Farm Bureau). Roughly 600 m bushels of soybeans a year.
lanes.mechanism: Gatún Lake is a rain-fed freshwater reservoir and every transit spends its water to the sea. An El Niño rainfall deficit in the Canal watershed lowers the lake, and the ACP rations transit slots and draft to protect both navigation and Panama City's drinking water.

live_2026.quote: cumulative rainfall across the Canal watershed has been 34% below the historical average, while watershed inflows have been 44% below their historical average for the same period
live_2026.el_nino_quote: forecasts indicate that the anticipated severity of the 2026-2027 El Niño event could further reduce precipitation and runoff during the remainder of the wet season
live_2026.draft: Maximum authorised draft of 14.63 m (48.0 ft) TFW in the Neopanamax locks postponed to 2 September 2026; the 14.48 m (47.5 ft) step postponed to 1 October 2026.
live_2026.signed: Boris Moreno Vásquez, Vice President for Operations
live_2026.date_note: The advisory gives two dates per step: when the restriction takes effect, and the booking dates it first applies to. Effective 21 Aug 2026 for booking dates from 4 Sept; effective 1 Sept 2026 for booking dates from 15 Sept. The slot counts here are keyed to the EFFECTIVE date.

precedent_2023.headline: The 2023-24 El Niño cut the canal from 36–38 transits a day to 18.
precedent_2023.lake: Gatún fell to 79.6 ft in August 2023 and by 1 January 2024 was at its lowest ever recorded level for that calendar date. The prior record low was 78.3 ft in May 2016 — also an El Niño.
precedent_2023.queue: 154–163 vessels waiting in August 2023, roughly 21-day waits. Grain vessels waited about 20 days by late November.
precedent_2023.grain: US Gulf grain routed to Asia via Panama collapsed from 80–85% of shipments in October 2022 to 9% in October 2023 and 0% in November 2023. CHS Inc. reported its own Panama share falling from 85% to 15% in a year.
precedent_2023.outturn: FY2024 deep-draft transits 9,944, down 21% on FY2023. FY2025 recovered to 13,404 — +34.8% against that deep-draft figure. The +19.3% the Authority headlines is computed on a different, all-transits denominator; the two numbers are not comparable and should not be presented as one series.

lanes.prior_events: Restrictions also followed the 2015-16 event (first weather-driven draft cut in about 20 years, from 8 September 2015) and the 2019 event (Panama's driest January in 106 years; draft cut in four steps from 48 ft to 44 ft).

sources.label: Panama Canal Authority — Advisories to Shipping

lanes.name: Amazon barge corridor (Madeira–Itacoatiara, Tapajós–Santarém)
lanes.food_role: Brazil's Northern Arc ports grew from 8% of national grain exports in 2010 to about 40% in 2023, handling roughly 34% of soybean and 42.5% of maize exports that year. Amaggi alone moves about 8 Mt/yr on its own river fleet.
lanes.mechanism: Grain moves from Mato Grosso by barge down the Madeira and Tapajós to transhipment ports. Low water forces convoys to cut loads or stop entirely.
lanes.events: Rio Negro at Manaus fell to 12.70 m on 26 October 2023, the lowest since records began in 1902, then to 12.66 m in 2024. The Madeira at Porto Velho hit 1.10 m in 2023 — lowest in a 56-year record — and 71 cm in September 2024. Rondônia's port authority suspended Madeira navigation on 23 September 2023; Tapajós convoys cut loads to about half.
lanes.attribution_caveat: World Weather Attribution (24 January 2024) is explicit and its finding cuts against the media shorthand: "El Niño reduced the amount of precipitation in the region by about the same amount as climate change; however, the strong drying trend was almost entirely due to increased global temperatures." The 2005 Amazon drought had essentially NO Pacific ENSO signal and was attributed to a warm tropical North Atlantic. Do not call these simply 'the El Niño droughts'.
lanes.counter_evidence: ANEC, the exporters' association, called the volumes affected "insignificant with no widespread trend", and Brazil still set record 2023 exports (soy ~99–101 Mt, +30% y/y). No aggregate stranded-tonnage figure exists — a genuine evidentiary gap.

lanes.name: Paraná–Paraguay waterway (Gran Rosario)
lanes.food_role: Gran Rosario handles about 75.7 Mt/yr of grain, oils and meals — roughly 80% of Argentina's grain and oilseed exports.
lanes.mechanism: Draft on the Paraná sets how much a Panamax can load at Rosario. Each foot of lost draft is 1,800–2,200 t of cargo left behind, so vessels must top off at Bahía Blanca or Quequén.
lanes.events: During the 2019/20–2022/23 triple-dip La Niña the Rosario gauge fell to 8 cm in May 2020 and the Paraná reached its lowest level since 1944 in October 2021. Panamax vessels loaded about 30% less grain. The 2020 episode cost exporters up to $244 m; the Bolsa de Comercio de Rosario put the March–August 2021 episode at $315 m.
lanes.attribution_caveat: THIS IS A LA NIÑA FAILURE, NOT AN EL NIÑO ONE. World Weather Attribution found La Niña — not climate change — the chief driver of the low Plata-basin rainfall, with up to >80% higher relative drought likelihood in some tributaries during La Niña.

sources.label: Carbon Brief — South American drought partly driven by triple-dip La Niña

lanes.name: Mississippi River barge corridor
lanes.food_role: The inland waterway system carries a large share of US grain to the Gulf for export. Barge freight is the marginal cost that sets Gulf basis.
lanes.mechanism: Low water cuts tow size and loading draft, so freight rates spike and grain backs up upriver.
lanes.events: Memphis hit a record −10.81 ft in October 2022; St. Louis barge spot rates reached an all-time $105.85/ton in the week of 11 October 2022, tows cut from 30–40 barges to 25. The record fell again to −11.52 ft in October 2023.
lanes.attribution_caveat: THE TWO EVENTS HAVE DIFFERENT CAUSES AND ONLY ONE IS AN ENSO STORY. 2022 fell in a La Niña (ASO ONI −0.9) and is consistent with a documented cold-Pacific mechanism (Munoz et al. 2023). 2023 coincided with a STRONG EL NIÑO (ASO +1.5) yet is NOT attributed to it — the textbook El Niño teleconnection would have made the lower basin WETTER. Jonathan Overpeck (Michigan) said the 2023 drought was "not caused by" El Niño, attributing it to a summer heat dome. NOAA notes the upper basin, which supplies ~90% of Memphis flow, responds to El Niño as a "toss-up". This lane is the page's counter-example: ENSO phase and hydrological outcome diverged.

sources.label: Munoz et al. 2023, Environ. Res. Climate
NOAA CPO — how El Niño flavors affect the Mississippi basin

lanes.name: Strait of Malacca
lanes.food_role: 25–30% of global seaborne trade; a record 94,301 transits in 2024.
lanes.mechanism: Indirect and unusual: El Niño drought drives Sumatra and Kalimantan peat fires, whose haze cuts navigational visibility in the strait.
lanes.events: The 2015-16 event drove severe fires (causal chain confirmed by NASA/PNAS) and haze cut visibility to as low as 200 m by September 2015.
lanes.attribution_caveat: No vessel-delay or tonnage figure was found for this episode. The mechanism is documented; the disruption is not quantified. Listed as weak for that reason.

lanes.name: Rhine (Kaub gauge)
lanes.mechanism: Low water at Kaub restricts barge loading; the 2018 event held below the critical 78 cm threshold for over 130 days.
lanes.attribution_caveat: NO ENSO LINK. Peer-reviewed attribution finds the driver is a persistent anticyclonic block over the eastern Atlantic and western Europe — the strongest 500 hPa anomaly since 1950 — and explicitly finds no simple causal relationship to ENSO when compared against other La Niña years. The Rhine is listed here so the page states the absence rather than leaving a reader to assume it.

sources.label: Environ. Res. Lett. 2023 — attribution of Rhine low-water

lanes.name: Suez Canal
lanes.food_role: 12–15% of world trade in a normal year.
lanes.attribution_caveat: NO ENSO LINK. Suez and Red Sea disruption since late 2023 is geopolitical. It is on this map only because it absorbed the grain Panama could not carry in 2023 — the two chokepoints are coupled by rerouting, not by climate.

lanes.name: Bab el-Mandeb
lanes.food_role: Red Sea gateway; the other half of the Suez routing.

lanes.name: Turkish Straits
lanes.food_role: Gateway for Black Sea grain — roughly 20% of global wheat exports (Chatham House, 2017 analysis). One of only two food chokepoints with no maritime alternative.
lanes.attribution_caveat: NO ENSO LINK. Governed by the Montreux Convention and by the war; transit economics here are political, not climatic.

sources.label: Chatham House — Chokepoints in global food trade
